paragraphs: Designing a new protein involves choosing both its three-dimensional structure and its amino-acid sequence. Common approaches handle these decisions in separate stages. That separation creates two problems: generated structures can differ in quality from the crystal structures used to train sequence designers, and sequence design cannot feed improvements back into structure generation.

CarbonNovo brings both decisions into a unified energy-based model. It combines a score-based generative model with Markov Random Fields to describe structure and sequence together. The two design components exchange information at every diffusion step, encouraging compatible pairs as generation proceeds. The framework can also incorporate protein language models to impose evolutionary constraints on the resulting proteins.

The reported evaluation finds improvements over two-stage methods in designability, novelty, sequence plausibility, and Rosetta Energy. These findings support the value of coordinating structure and sequence throughout generation. The central contribution is a way for the two design processes to influence one another, addressing the separation that motivates the work.
icml-2024-carbonnovo-joint-design-of-pro.tldr: CarbonNovo jointly generates protein structures and sequences through interacting design components, improving several reported measures over two-stage methods.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks incorporate differential equations into their training objective through a residual term. Successfully minimizing that objective is a major part of making the networks useful. This paper examines why training can be difficult by studying the loss landscape, especially the ill-conditioning associated with the differential operators in that residual.

Ill-conditioning means that the optimization problem responds very differently along different directions, making progress difficult for an optimizer. The authors theoretically connect ill-conditioned differential operators to ill-conditioning in the network's loss. They also compare Adam, L-BFGS, and a combination of the two, finding that the combined approach performs better in their comparison.

The paper introduces NysNewton-CG, a second-order optimizer that significantly improves the reported PINN performance. Its theoretical analysis also explains benefits of combining first- and second-order optimization methods. Together, these results identify optimization geometry as an important source of training difficulty and offer more effective strategies for addressing it, with potential benefits for solving difficult partial differential equations.
icml-2024-challenges-in-training-pinns-a.tldr: The paper links PINN training difficulties to ill-conditioned losses and develops optimization strategies that improve reported performance.

paragraphs: A model that learns several basic operations might also learn to combine them into many more complex operations. This paper investigates that possibility using synthetic tasks with clearly defined component functions. Because the data-generating process is controlled and interpretable, the experiments can directly examine how autoregressive Transformers learn and combine those components.

The experiments show that these models can learn compositional structure from relatively little training data and generalize to exponentially or even combinatorially many functions. Producing intermediate outputs improves generalization to unseen compositions compared with producing no intermediate outputs. This suggests that making intermediate results part of generation can help models carry learned operations into new combinations.

The results also reveal a constraint: biases in the ordering of compositions during training can leave models unable to combine some functions. An examination of the networks suggests that attention layers select which capability to apply, while feed-forward layers carry it out. That division is presented as an observed interpretation, alongside empirical evidence that training structure strongly affects compositional generalization.
icml-2024-compositional-capabilities-of-.tldr: Controlled synthetic experiments show that Transformers can generalize across many function compositions, with intermediate outputs and training order affecting success.

paragraphs: Strong video question-answering scores do not necessarily show that a model combines language and video effectively. This paper investigates that distinction by deliberately weakening the interaction between modalities. Its QUAG probe is lightweight and has no learned parameters, allowing the authors to examine models and datasets together through the effect of impaired modality fusion.

The authors find that models retain high performance on many datasets without relying on multimodal representations. They further test this result with QUAG-attention, a restricted replacement for self-attention. It achieves similar performance with substantially fewer multiplication operations and no fine-tuning. These findings raise questions about how much existing benchmark performance depends on tightly integrating video and language.

To test that integration more directly, the authors introduce CLAVI, constructed by augmenting real-world videos to require strong coupling between modalities. Most evaluated models perform near a trivial level on this dataset. The combined evidence points to a gap between success on existing datasets and the ability to learn the highly coupled representations that CLAVI tests.
icml-2024-dissecting-multimodality-in-vi.tldr: Impairing video–language interaction reveals that many VideoQA benchmark scores conceal weaknesses in tightly coupled multimodal reasoning.

paragraphs: Derivative-free optimization searches for good solutions using function evaluations rather than directly available derivatives. When those evaluations are noisy, estimating a useful gradient from sampled values becomes difficult. This paper develops a smoothing method that accounts for the objective having different curvature in different directions, extending ball and Gaussian smoothing approaches.

The algorithm changes the shape of its smoothing kernel as optimization proceeds. It adapts that shape to approximate the objective's Hessian around a local optimum, using local curvature to guide the smoothing. The stated benefit is a substantial reduction in the error of gradient estimates obtained from noisy samples. The mechanism therefore targets the reliability of the directional information used during optimization.

Numerical experiments on artificial problems demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The authors also apply it to tuning solvers for NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, where it improves performance over the compared heuristic derivative-free and Bayesian optimization methods. These results support adapting smoothing geometry to the objective in the noisy optimization settings studied.
icml-2024-dynamic-anisotropic-smoothing-.tldr: Adapting a smoothing kernel to local curvature improves gradient estimation from noisy evaluations and performance in reported optimization experiments.

paragraphs: Early classification aims to label an incoming sequence before observing all of it, while keeping accuracy close to the full-sequence classifier. This paper develops a statistical stopping framework that can be attached to any sequential classifier. Its stopping rule is calibrated from data and provides finite-sample, distribution-free control over the accuracy gap.

The authors first build on Learn-then-Test calibration to control the gap on average across independent, identically distributed instances. However, that average guarantee can coexist with an excessively large gap among early stopping times. Their main contribution strengthens the target by controlling the accuracy gap conditionally on accumulated halt times, addressing a weakness that the marginal average can hide.

Numerical experiments demonstrate the framework's usefulness and applicability. In the reported results, early stopping reduces the number of classification timesteps by up to 94% while retaining rigorous accuracy-gap control. The contribution connects a practical stopping decision to a calibrated statistical guarantee, with special attention to accuracy losses associated with stopping early.
icml-2024-early-time-classification-with.tldr: A calibrated stopping framework controls early-classification accuracy loss and cuts timesteps by up to 94% in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning must accommodate participants who may prefer different output models. Earlier fairness work used core stability to provide guarantees for any subset of participants, but required strong assumptions about their numerical utilities. This paper changes the basis of comparison from the magnitude of utility to the ordinal rank of a model in participants' preferences.

Using rankings, the authors adapt the proportional veto core from social choice theory to federated learning. They prove that models satisfying the resulting PVC stability criterion exist across very general learning settings. In particular, the existence result allows non-convex model sets and loss functions that are neither convex nor concave, broadening the settings covered by the fairness formulation.

The authors also introduce Rank-Core-Fed, a distributed algorithm for training a PVC-stable model. Experiments across different datasets show better fairness than the evaluated baselines. The paper thus connects a ranking-based fairness definition with an existence guarantee and a training method, offering an alternative to utility-based guarantees whose assumptions can be impractical.
icml-2024-fair-federated-learning-via-th.tldr: Rank-Core-Fed uses ranking-based fairness to train federated models under a stability notion that exists in broad, including non-convex, settings.

paragraphs: Learning a new decision-making task from a few demonstrations is harder than recognizing a new pattern in a fixed input. An agent's actions and environmental randomness can lead to unfamiliar states, sometimes with no recovery. The paper uses an illustrative example to show why applying Transformers naively does not produce in-context learning of new sequential tasks.

The authors instead train on sequences of trajectories with particular distributional properties. They investigate which design choices improve adaptation without changing model weights. In their experiments, larger models and datasets help, as do greater task diversity, environmental stochasticity, and trajectory burstiness. These findings make the organization and variety of training experience central to learning new tasks from context.

Training on large, diverse offline datasets enables the resulting model to learn new MiniHack and Procgen tasks from only a handful of demonstrations, without weight updates. The results demonstrate in-context adaptation in those sequential environments and show that the training distribution matters substantially for obtaining it, beyond simply choosing a Transformer architecture.
icml-2024-generalization-to-new-sequenti.tldr: Training Transformers on suitably structured, diverse trajectories enables adaptation to new sequential tasks from a few demonstrations without weight updates.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning can imitate an expert using fewer demonstrations and with greater resistance to compounding errors than behavioral cloning. Its cost is repeatedly solving an expensive reinforcement learning problem. Much of that effort can go toward policies far from the expert's behavior, making the inner policy search unnecessarily demanding.

This paper uses hybrid reinforcement learning, combining online experience with expert data, to focus that search. Expert examples direct learning toward good states and reduce the exploration needed to obtain a strong policy. The method does not require resetting the learner to arbitrary environment states. Formally, the authors reduce inverse reinforcement learning to finding an expert-competitive policy rather than a globally optimal one.

That reduction supports both model-free and model-based hybrid algorithms with policy performance guarantees while reducing interaction in the inner search loop. On a suite of continuous control tasks, the approaches are substantially more sample efficient than standard inverse reinforcement learning and several other baselines. The results support using expert data throughout policy search to preserve imitation benefits with less exploration.
icml-2024-hybrid-inverse-reinforcement-l.tldr: Hybrid inverse reinforcement learning combines expert data and online experience to reduce exploration while retaining policy performance guarantees.

paragraphs: A controller can perform well from the initial states used in training yet behave differently from unfamiliar starting points. This paper asks how policy gradient's implicit bias affects that extrapolation. The concern is which controller gradient-based learning selects when training success alone does not determine behavior on unseen initial states.

The theoretical analysis focuses on the Linear Quadratic Regulator problem. It establishes that extrapolation depends on how much exploration the system induces when starting from the training states. This connects performance on new starting conditions to the experience generated from familiar ones. The initial states matter through the system behavior they cause during training, rather than merely as a list of starting examples.

Experiments corroborate the theory and demonstrate its conclusions beyond the linear-quadratic setting, including nonlinear systems controlled by neural networks. The authors further hypothesize that choosing training initial states in an informed way could substantially improve real-world control. That proposed direction follows from the findings, while remaining a hypothesis about broader practical improvement.
icml-2024-implicit-bias-of-policy-gradie.tldr: The analysis connects policy-gradient extrapolation to unseen initial states with the exploration induced by training starting states.

paragraphs: Feedback Alignment methods train neural networks using biologically inspired local rules that reduce communication between layers. Their potential includes distributed and privacy-aware learning, but their impact has been constrained by multiclass classification difficulties and an incomplete explanation of alignment. This paper develops a unified framework for understanding how the alignment mechanism operates.

The central theoretical contribution is a conservation law connecting changes in synaptic weights to implicit regularization that maintains alignment with the gradient. Experiments support this connection. The authors also introduce sufficient conditions for convergence through a property called alignment dominance. These conditions identify circumstances where convergence follows; they are not presented as requirements that every convergent process must satisfy.

An empirical analysis finds that better alignment can improve Feedback Alignment performance on complex multiclass tasks. Together, the theoretical and experimental results make the behavior of these learning rules easier to interpret. They also provide a foundation for developing improved algorithms by connecting training performance to the mechanism that keeps updates aligned with the gradient.
icml-2024-implicit-regularization-in-fee.tldr: A conservation law explains implicit regularization in Feedback Alignment, alongside sufficient convergence conditions and evidence that better alignment can improve classification.

paragraphs: Batched linear bandits require balancing exploration and reward while organizing learning into batches. The paper introduces E⁴, which proceeds through exploration, estimation, elimination, and exploitation. Its objective is to achieve strong regret guarantees while limiting batch complexity, so performance is assessed both by reward lost and by the number of batches required.

With an appropriate exploration rate, E⁴ achieves finite-time minimax-optimal regret using O(log log T) batches and asymptotically optimal regret using three batches as the horizon T grows. A lower bound shows that asymptotically optimal linear contextual bandit algorithms require at least three batches in expectation in that limit. This establishes matching asymptotic batch complexity alongside optimal regret.

Another exploration-rate choice provides an instance-dependent regret bound with at most O(log T) batches while preserving minimax and asymptotic optimality. Experiments cover randomly generated problems and challenging End of Optimism instances. Across these evaluations, E⁴ outperforms the compared baselines in regret, batch complexity, and computational efficiency, complementing the theoretical guarantees with empirical evidence.
icml-2024-optimal-batched-linear-bandits.tldr: E⁴ combines optimal regret guarantees with low batch complexity, including asymptotically optimal regret using three batches.

paragraphs: Plug-and-play image restoration combines a physical observation model with a neural network that regularizes the recovered image. Conventional methods apply a denoiser repeatedly as the images become less noisy. The paper highlights that this use differs from diffusion-based approaches, which apply the denoiser to images after noise has been added again.

SNORE changes the restoration procedure so that the denoiser only receives images with an appropriate noise level. The method is built around an explicit stochastic regularization objective, leading to a stochastic gradient descent algorithm for ill-posed inverse problems. This gives the denoising operation a defined role within the optimization rather than relying only on repeated application during restoration.

The authors provide a convergence analysis for the algorithm and an annealing extension. In experiments on deblurring and inpainting, SNORE is competitive with state-of-the-art methods in both numerical evaluation and visual quality. The results support a restoration framework that aligns denoiser inputs with the intended noise level while retaining effective image reconstruction.
icml-2024-plug-and-play-image-restoratio.tldr: SNORE uses stochastic regularization to apply denoisers at appropriate noise levels, with convergence analysis and competitive image restoration results.

paragraphs: AI governance proposals depend on technical capabilities to make their goals achievable. This position paper argues that there are significant gaps between what governance seeks to accomplish and what current technical tools can support. As governments pursue regulation and other interventions, those gaps affect the practical foundations of proposed policy actions.

The authors survey policy documents from public-sector institutions in the EU, the US, and China. Their analysis identifies disconnects between the technical requirements of proposed actions and the current state of the art. This makes the relationship between policy ambitions and technical readiness the central object of study, linking governance proposals to the capabilities needed to enact them.

The paper calls for closer integration of AI and machine-learning researchers into governance in two ways. Researchers should help develop tools that address gaps in the technical basis of regulatory action, and governing institutions should gain more technical expertise to inform their decisions. The argument treats research capacity and institutional talent as complementary ingredients of effective AI governance.
icml-2024-position-technical-research-an.tldr: The paper argues that effective AI governance needs technical research and institutional expertise to bridge gaps between policy ambitions and available tools.

paragraphs: As AI enters settings shaped by human behavior, researchers and policymakers need useful ways to describe acceptable conduct. This position paper turns to the American legal system's reasonable person standard. That standard evaluates behavior by considering what a reasonable person would have done in comparable circumstances, making context central to the judgment.

The authors explain how reasonableness is defined and applied across key legal areas, using illustrative cases. They then consider how the standard could apply to AI behavior in those areas and contexts. The proposal draws on society's existing approaches to evaluating human conduct to help identify behaviors worth developing and examining in AI systems.

For alignment research, the suggested value is in turning understandings of reasonable behavior into technical goals for model development, probing, and stress testing. The paper argues that the standard offers useful guidance for those activities. Its contribution is a proposed connection between legal reasoning about human conduct and the practical question of what behavior AI researchers should seek and evaluate.
icml-2024-position-the-reasonable-person.tldr: The paper proposes the legal reasonable person standard as guidance for developing and testing context-appropriate AI behavior.

paragraphs: Statistical generalization theory helps explain why models perform well on unseen data, but this position paper argues that it cannot by itself explain all desirable language-model capabilities. The authors call for a change in theoretical perspective, motivated by cases where similar predictive performance coexists with substantially different model behavior.

Their central argument concerns non-identifiability in autoregressive probabilistic models. Models separated by zero or nearly zero KL divergence, and thus equivalent test loss in the argument, can still behave differently. Mathematical examples and empirical observations illustrate the issue for zero-shot rule extrapolation, in-context learning, and fine-tunability. The in-context learning case is described specifically as approximate non-identifiability.

These cases challenge the idea that good test loss is enough to explain a model's ability to follow new rules, learn from context, or adapt through fine-tuning. The paper reviews research directions involving generalization measures suited to language models, transferability, and inductive biases. Its position is that these capabilities need theoretical explanations beyond conventional statistical generalization alone.
icml-2024-position-understanding-llms-re.tldr: The paper argues that equivalent test loss can hide major behavioral differences, so explaining LLM capabilities requires more than statistical generalization.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving federated learning must account for both how data are distributed and whether the coordinating server can be trusted. This paper studies those issues within stochastic convex optimization. It addresses centralized federated systems under both trusted and untrusted server scenarios, placing privacy and optimization efficiency within the same analysis.

The authors devise methods that provide differential privacy while maintaining optimal convergence rates for homogeneous and heterogeneous data distributions. The distinction matters because their stated results cover both similar and differing distributions across participants. The optimization framework also defines the scope of the contribution: these guarantees are developed for the stochastic convex setting considered in the paper.

The approach builds on a recent stochastic optimization technique and has linear computational complexity comparable to non-private federated learning methods. It also reduces gradient obfuscation. Taken together, the stated results address the practical cost of adding privacy: the methods combine privacy guarantees, convergence performance, and computational efficiency across different server trust environments and participant data distributions.
icml-2024-private-and-federated-stochast.tldr: The paper develops differentially private federated convex optimization methods with optimal convergence and linear computational complexity across server trust settings.

paragraphs: Preference-based alignment depends on comparisons that can be incorrect or ambiguous. This paper studies policy optimization when preference labels are randomly flipped, focusing on direct preference optimization. DPO uses a Bradley-Terry-Luce preference model, making the effect of corrupted comparisons an important question for the policy learned from them.

The authors introduce a loss that removes the noise's bias on average. Their robust DPO method has a theoretical guarantee under a log-linear policy parameterization and good feature coverage from the supervised fine-tuned policy. With flip rate ε below one half, parameter dimension d, and dataset size n, its suboptimality gap scales as O((1/(1−2ε))√(d/n)). The bound improves with more data and worsens as noise approaches one half.

Experiments on IMDb sentiment generation and Anthropic's helpful-harmless dataset find that robust DPO handles noisy preference labels better than ordinary DPO and the compared practitioner heuristics. The contribution combines an explicit random-flip model, a loss correction, and conditional performance guarantees, providing a theoretical basis for the observed robustness.
icml-2024-provably-robust-dpo-aligning-l.tldr: Robust DPO corrects preference-flip bias on average and offers conditional theoretical guarantees alongside improved empirical noise robustness.

paragraphs: Image-GPT applies autoregressive learning to images by predicting upcoming pixels. This paper revisits that approach with two changes intended to produce stronger visual representations. The first replaces raw-pixel prediction with prediction of semantic tokens, shifting the learning target toward higher-level visual content instead of individual pixel values.

The second change adds prediction of visible tokens alongside prediction of the next tokens. The resulting method, D-iGPT, therefore supplements the sequential prediction task with an additional objective over content already visible to the model. The authors report that the approach is particularly effective when its semantic tokens come from discriminatively trained models such as CLIP.

Extensive experiments support D-iGPT as a strong visual representation learner. Using publicly available training datasets and a vanilla ViT-H, it reaches 90.0% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K. The paper also reports strong generalization on a downstream task. These findings support revising both what an autoregressive image model predicts and which token positions contribute to its learning objective.
icml-2024-rejuvenating-image-gpt-as-stro.tldr: D-iGPT strengthens autoregressive visual learning by predicting semantic and visible tokens, reaching 90.0% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with a vanilla ViT-H.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning must connect actions to consequences that may arrive much later. Monte Carlo targets span long delays but can have high variance when outcomes are random. Temporal-difference learning reduces variance by bootstrapping from existing estimates, introducing bias that can require many updates to correct. TD(λ) offers a way to navigate this tradeoff.

Chunked-TD uses a learned model's predicted transition probabilities to compute λ-return targets. Its motivation is history compression: near-deterministic portions of an agent's trajectory can be treated as chunks, allowing credit to move across them more quickly. Where needed, the method still bootstraps. The compression depends on predictability in the combined interaction between the environment and the policy.

The authors propose versions that can operate online and show that they solve some problems much faster than conventional TD(λ). They also describe Chunked-TD as less vulnerable to model inaccuracies than other model-based credit-assignment approaches. The findings support using learned predictability to decide how to propagate credit, while preserving bootstrapping where it remains useful.
icml-2024-sequence-compression-speeds-up.tldr: Chunked-TD uses predicted transition probabilities to compress predictable trajectory segments and accelerate credit assignment on some problems.

paragraphs: Generating tokens with large language models can be limited by moving data rather than by computation alone. The paper highlights this bottleneck for applications that combine long input sequences with large batches. Attention must access cached history during generation, making the amount of transferred data an important target for improving inference throughput.

SparQ Attention addresses that target by selectively fetching cached history inside attention layers. The technique uses memory bandwidth more efficiently and can be applied directly to existing language models during inference. It requires neither changes to their pre-training setup nor additional fine-tuning, so its use does not depend on retraining a model specifically for the method.

Evaluations cover Llama 2 and 3, Mistral, Gemma, and Pythia across a range of downstream tasks. The reported savings reach up to eightfold in attention data transfers without substantial accuracy drops. That result concerns attention's transfer requirements, demonstrating that selective access can reduce a key inference bottleneck while retaining accuracy in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-sparq-attention-bandwidth-effi.tldr: SparQ Attention selectively fetches cached history, reducing attention data transfers by up to eightfold without substantial accuracy drops in evaluated models.

paragraphs: Using a language model as a decision-making agent requires choices about the model, its prompts, and whether it should reason explicitly or introspect. STEER proposes a methodology for assessing the economic rationality of such agents. The aim is to make evaluation of their decision behavior systematic enough to inform questions about reliability.

The authors begin with economic research on rational decision making and organize it into fine-grained behavioral elements. They also identify dependencies among those elements. A proposed benchmark distribution quantitatively scores model performance on them, and a user-supplied rubric turns those scores into a rationality report card. The rubric connects the measured behaviors to the user's evaluation priorities.

The paper reports a large empirical study involving 14 language models. It characterizes their rational behavior and examines the influence of model size. The contribution is an assessment framework that separates rationality into explicit components, together with evidence about existing models. This gives model and agent-design comparisons a structured basis grounded in the surveyed economic concepts.
icml-2024-steer-assessing-the-economic-r.tldr: STEER evaluates language-model agents through fine-grained economic rationality criteria and user-weighted report cards, with a study of 14 models.

paragraphs: TabLog addresses adapting a tabular prediction model to a new data distribution using only unlabeled target data and no access to source data. Tables contain heterogeneous features with complex dependencies, which makes this setting difficult for existing adaptation methods. The paper approaches those dependencies through an ensemble of logical rules.

Its central assumption is that the rules' logical structure stays invariant across the distribution shift. Numerical parameters within the rules and the weights assigned to them may change. TabLog discretizes numerical features, models relationships between different feature types, and introduces a contrastive loss to handle the shift. A logical neural network representation supports end-to-end training and test-time adaptation.

Across several benchmark datasets, TabLog matches or improves upon state-of-the-art tabular adaptation methods. The approach provides a specific division between what is preserved and what is adapted: logical relationships supply the stable structure, while numerical settings and rule importance can respond to the target domain. Its stated assumption is therefore central to how the adaptation mechanism is organized.
icml-2024-tablog-test-time-adaptation-fo.tldr: TabLog adapts tabular models using unlabeled target data, assuming logical rule structure stays stable while numerical parameters and rule weights change.

paragraphs: Measuring how much a neural network memorizes its training examples can be computationally expensive. Earlier empirical work connected memorization to input loss curvature, measured by the trace of the loss Hessian with respect to inputs. That curvature measure was reported to be roughly three orders of magnitude cheaper than computing a formal memorization score.

This paper develops theoretical links behind that empirical connection and extends them to differential privacy. The authors derive an upper bound on memorization involving both privacy and input loss curvature. They also show that input loss curvature is upper-bounded by the differential privacy parameter. These are bounding relationships connecting the quantities, rather than claims that they are identical measures.

Experiments with deep models on CIFAR and ImageNet show a strong correlation between the theoretical predictions and observed results. The work therefore gives theoretical support to a computationally attractive way of studying memorization, while connecting that analysis to privacy. Its contribution brings previously observed curvature relationships into a framework that also accounts for differential privacy.
icml-2024-unveiling-privacy-memorization.tldr: The paper derives bounds linking memorization, input loss curvature, and differential privacy, supported by experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet.

paragraphs: A language model trained against a reward model can exploit flaws in that reward signal, earning high scores without satisfying the underlying preference. This paper identifies two challenges behind such reward hacking: the distribution changes during reinforcement learning, and human preferences can be inconsistent. WARM aims to make the reward model more reliable under both conditions.

The method fine-tunes several reward models and then averages their weights. It builds on the observation that fine-tuned models sharing the same pre-training remain linearly mode connected. Weight averaging produces a more efficient alternative to ensembling their predictions, while the reported results show improved reliability under distribution shifts and greater robustness to preference inconsistencies.

Experiments examine summarization using both best-of-N selection and reinforcement learning. WARM improves overall output quality and alignment; one reported policy trained with WARM wins 79.4% of comparisons against a policy trained with a single reward model. These findings support weight averaging as a practical way to strengthen reward modeling in the evaluated alignment settings.
icml-2024-warm-on-the-benefits-of-weight.tldr: WARM averages fine-tuned reward-model weights to improve robustness and summarization alignment more efficiently than prediction ensembling.
